result: {"decisions":[{"point":"D2","problem":"How to evaluate whether AI can cause catastrophic harm, given uncertainty about which specific cognitive capabilities are limiting.","did":"They chose end-to-end, threat-model-driven task evaluations built as a chain from real-world threat to measurable proxies, rather than measuring isolated cognitive abilities.","alternatives_named":["directly identifying the key missing cognitive capability and measuring that","generic ML benchmarks","academic fine-grained questions about specific reasoning"],"stated_reason":"It is hard to know the limiting capabilities, and going straight to a particular dimension risks it not being linked to the real-world outcomes of concern; benchmarks also saturate quickly and are poor proxies for models.","quote":"But I think we do actually want to work backwards from something that we think is a better proxy for danger and see if we can distill that into some more specific underlying capability"},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to elicit model capabilities without fooling oneself that the evaluators' own prompt-engineering supplies the capability.","did":"They advocate doing all elicitation on a dev set and evaluating on a separate test set, with generalization gap matching that between test set and the real-world target.","alternatives_named":["task-specific elicitation on the evaluated tasks","IID split versus artificially adding distributional shift"],"stated_reason":"Task-specific or narrowly targeted elicitation can put the answer in, so the held-out test keeps the evaluation fair.","quote":"So the way we think you should actually do this is you do all your elicitation against a dev set and then you evaluate on a separate test set so it’s fair."},{"point":"D5","problem":"How to interpret the GPT-4 evaluation results when the evaluators lacked fine-tuning access and the model failed at scary tasks.","did":"They patched over problems they expected to be fixable soon (e.g., browsing via a human-simulated agent, reminders, hallucinated text) and treated continued failure as a soft upper bound with added margin.","alternatives_named":["evaluating the model as-is without patching","using existing tools for blind users"],"stated_reason":"Without patching, all tasks fail for the same reason, giving no information about what the next hurdle is; fixable limitations are likely to be removed soon.","quote":"You don’t want to be in the situation where all of your tasks are failing for the same reason, that you think is a thing that might change quickly, because then you’re just not getting any information"},{"point":"D5","problem":"Whether current models might be deliberately sandbagging evaluations.","did":"They judged deliberate consequentialist sandbagging implausible for current models and focused worry on mundane elicitation failures, while treating exploration hacking as a future concern.","alternatives_named":["worrying about deliberate scheming sandbagging now","gradient hacking"],"stated_reason":"Doing so would require advanced single-forward-pass reasoning beyond long chain-of-thought, implying implausible capability discontinuities.","quote":"They’re not good enough. It just seems like they would have to be doing things in a single forward pass in a single token that are very advanced compared to what they can do in long chain of thought"},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to test whether a model is sandbagging or hiding capabilities when direct elicitation may fail.","did":"They propose fine-tuning on human-like policies/supervised data to show the capability, assuming no gradient hacking, and distinguishing knowing the capabilities from knowing whether you know them.","alternatives_named":["prompting alone","classification data set the model cannot fit as an upper bound"],"stated_reason":"If the model can be fine-tuned to show the capability, you must assume it has it; this works unless the capability is too superhuman to have example data.","quote":"Then if you assume they can’t gradient hack, then for anything on which you can construct a policy by which the model should be able to do the task, you can then just fine-tune it on that."},{"point":"D1","problem":"Which threat models to prioritize for evaluation given limited capacity.","did":"They prioritized AI R&D and autonomous replication/adaptation evaluations over domain-specific ones like CBRN or persuasion.","alternatives_named":["bioweapon evaluations","persuasion evaluations","CBRN evaluations"],"stated_reason":"These are the scariest, soonest threats and cover more risk per eval; domain-specific work needs expertise others have and ML tasks avoid two-team hiring difficulties.","quote":"Yeah, and that it gets more things with one thing, rather than having to look at all of the different-"},{"point":"D1","problem":"How to structure red lines and buffers so evaluations give warning before dangerous capability levels.","did":"They emphasized building a smooth y-axis of dangerous capability and either setting a red line then adjusting down by a buffer, or building the furthest-out eval confidently preceding the risk.","alternatives_named":["create the red line then adjust down for buffer","create the furthest-out eval that still clearly comes before the risk","modify tasks or agent assistance to define the buffer gap"],"stated_reason":"The bottleneck to scaling-law extrapolation is a good y-axis whose increments mean the same thing; random benchmark scaling laws don't relate to risk.","quote":"There’s two ways you could think about it: one is first, you create the red line and then you figure out how much buffer, you adjust down from that."},{"point":"D1","problem":"How to design lab policy commitments: prescriptive mitigations versus lab-specific red lines.","did":"They shifted from prescriptive, situation-specific mitigation requirements to letting each lab set its own red lines with general pressure to improve them.","alternatives_named":["prescriptive mitigations per situation","complicated conditionals","safety case with review process"],"stated_reason":"Labs differ in situations and costs, and uncertain capability profiles meant prescriptive rules were either overly complex or overly conservative.","quote":"So that’s why we ended up going to more [towards] each lab can say what their red lines are and then there’s some general pressure and ratchet to hopefully make those better."},{"point":"D4","problem":"Whether to continue building a classification data set that upper-bounds model capability.","did":"They tried creating a classification dataset capturing hard parts of tasks but moved on to other work because it was hard.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"It was hard, though it would give stronger guarantees about the model not being able to do the task.","quote":"And in particular, something that we tried to do for a while, but ended up moving on to other things, which was hard, was creating a classification data set that captures the hard parts of doing a particular task"}]}
